question: What is the first step the manual recommends to make sure your motorcycle won't let you down on the highway?
choice_a: Buy the most powerful motorcycle available
choice_b: Add as many aftermarket accessories as possible
choice_d: Start with the right motorcycle for you -- it should fit you well
explanation: To make sure your motorcycle won't let you down, the manual advises you to start with the right motorcycle for you -- it should fit you well, and you should read the owner's manual, be familiar with the controls, and check it before every ride.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.9, 'Know Your Motorcycle'

question: When choosing a motorcycle that "fits" you, what should be true while you are seated on it?
choice_a: Your feet should reach the ground, and the controls should be easy to operate
choice_b: Only your toes need to touch the ground
choice_c: You should be unable to reach the handlebars comfortably
choice_d: The seat height is irrelevant to fit
explanation: Your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate; smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners to operate.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.9, 'The Right Motorcycle for You'

question: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have which of the following?
choice_b: Headlight, taillight, brake light, front and rear brakes, turn signals, horn, and two mirrors
explanation: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have a headlight, taillight and brake light, front and rear brakes, turn signals, a horn, and two mirrors.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.9, 'The Right Motorcycle for You'

question: What does the manual say about crashes and beginning riders who borrow or lend motorcycles?
choice_a: Borrowed motorcycles are always safer than one's own
choice_b: Experience level makes no difference in crash risk
choice_c: Crashes are more likely to occur among beginning riders, especially in the first months of riding, and riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds risk
choice_d: Lending a motorcycle removes all liability from the owner
explanation: Crashes are more likely to occur among beginning riders, especially in the first months of riding. Riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds risk, so borrowers should get familiar with it away from traffic, and lenders should make sure borrowers are licensed and know how to ride.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.10, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: According to the manual, more than half of all crashes involve riders with how much experience on their motorcycle?
choice_a: More than five years of experience
choice_c: Experience level has no bearing on crash rates
choice_d: Less than five months of experience
explanation: More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.10, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: Before taking an unfamiliar motorcycle out on the street, what should a rider do first?
choice_a: Review the owner's manual and become completely familiar with the motorcycle's controls
choice_b: Skip inspection since it wastes time
explanation: Riders should make sure they are completely familiar with the motorcycle before taking it out on the street, including reviewing the owner's manual -- particularly important with a borrowed motorcycle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.10, 'Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls'

question: When using an unfamiliar motorcycle, what should a rider locate and be able to operate without looking?
choice_b: The turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve, and engine cut-off switch
explanation: If using an unfamiliar motorcycle, find out where everything is -- particularly the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve, and engine cut-off switch -- and be able to find and operate these items without looking for them.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.10, 'Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls'

question: How should a rider approach an unfamiliar or borrowed motorcycle when first riding it?
choice_a: Ride at full speed immediately to get a feel for it
choice_c: Ride very cautiously, accelerate gently, take turns more slowly, and leave extra room for stopping
explanation: No matter how experienced a rider may be, they should ride very cautiously and be aware of surroundings on any new or unfamiliar motorcycle -- accelerating gently, taking turns more slowly, and leaving extra room for stopping.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.10, 'Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls'

question: What is the primary source of information about how a motorcycle should be inspected and maintained?
choice_b: Word of mouth from other riders
choice_c: There is no reliable source; guesswork is fine
explanation: The primary source of information about how a motorcycle should be inspected and maintained is its owner's manual, which a rider should absorb fully.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: What convenient reminder, developed by the Motorcycle Safety Foundation, helps riders remember what to check before every ride?
explanation: T-CLOCS is a convenient reminder developed by the MSF for a pre-ride inspection; a T-CLOCS tear-out checklist is included at the back of the manual.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: In the T-CLOCS pre-ride inspection, what does the "T" stand for?
explanation: In T-CLOCS, "T" stands for Tires and Wheels -- checking inflation pressure, treadwear, and general condition of the sidewalls and tread surface.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: In the T-CLOCS pre-ride inspection, what does the "C" (first C) stand for?
choice_c: Controls -- checking that the clutch, throttle, and horn operate smoothly and the throttle snaps back when released
explanation: In T-CLOCS, "C" stands for Controls: make sure the clutch and throttle operate smoothly, the throttle snaps back to fully closed when released, and the horn works.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: During the T-CLOCS "Lights and Electrics" check, what should a rider verify about the mirrors?
choice_a: That they are removed before riding
choice_b: That only the left mirror needs to be checked
choice_c: Mirrors are not part of a pre-ride inspection
choice_d: That they are clean, tight, and adjusted so the rider can see the lane behind and the lane next to them
explanation: As part of the Lights and Electrics check, clean and adjust mirrors before starting so the rider can see the lane behind and the lane next to them.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: During the T-CLOCS "Oil and Other Fluids" check, what should a rider do regarding the fuel valve before starting out, if equipped?
choice_a: Be sure the fuel valve is open, since a closed valve may let the motorcycle start on residual fuel in the lines but stall once they empty
choice_b: Always leave the fuel valve closed while riding
choice_c: Fuel valves do not need to be checked
choice_d: Only check the fuel valve after a crash
explanation: Be sure the fuel valve is open, if equipped, before starting out; with the fuel valve closed the motorcycle may start with only the fuel still in the lines but will stall once the lines are empty.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.11, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: In the T-CLOCS "S" check for Stands, what should a rider confirm about the side stand?
choice_a: That it is removed entirely before every ride
choice_b: That it operates smoothly and the spring holds it tightly in the up position while riding
choice_c: Side stands do not require any maintenance
choice_d: That it is left down while riding for stability
explanation: Ensure the side stand operates smoothly and that the spring holds it tightly in the up position; if equipped, the center stand should also be held firmly against the frame whenever the motorcycle is moving.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.12, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: According to the "Know Your Responsibilities" section, is a crash usually a matter of pure chance with no fault involved?
choice_a: Yes, crashes are always entirely unforeseeable and blameless
choice_b: Responsibility only ever belongs to the other driver
choice_c: No -- in traffic, most people involved in a crash should probably claim some responsibility for what takes place
choice_d: Responsibility only matters for insurance purposes
explanation: "Accident" implies an unforeseen event without fault, but in traffic that is often not the case -- most people involved in a crash should probably claim some responsibility for what takes place.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.12, 'Know Your Responsibilities'

question: To lessen the chances of a crash, the manual advises riders to do all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: Be visible by wearing proper clothing and using the headlight
choice_b: Communicate intentions using signals and lane position
choice_c: Maintain an adequate space cushion and search 12 seconds ahead
choice_d: Assume that other drivers will always yield the right of way
explanation: As a rider you can't be sure that other operators will see you or yield the right of way, so the manual advises being visible, communicating intentions, maintaining a space cushion, searching ahead, identifying hazards, and being prepared to act.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.12, 'Know Your Responsibilities'
